items.headline: Trump 'Willing to Wait a Few Days'; Moratorium Range Converges to 12-15 Years; Pakistan Army Chief to Tehran; Deal Track Live but Witkoff Dismantlement Demand Maximalist; Hormuz Day 84
items.summary: Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson confirmed May 21 that Tehran has received the latest US proposal and is reviewing it. President Trump stated he is willing to wait 'a few more days' — the same revealed patience preference that led him to hold the May 19 planned strike at Gulf allies' request. Pakistan continues to mediate direct and indirect exchanges; Pakistan's Army Chief is expected to travel to Tehran for direct engagement, representing the most substantive diplomatic escalation of the mediation channel since Vance's Islamabad visit in April. The moratorium duration negotiating range has shifted materially in reporting: whereas the public framing through May 20 described Iran's offer at 5 years and the US demand at 20 years, multiple sources now indicate the actual negotiating range is 'at least 12 years' with '15 years as a likely landing spot' — a 3-year negotiating margin rather than a 15-year gap. This is structurally significant: it represents convergence from maximalist positions toward a potential middle ground, and it implies that prior 'unbridgeable gap' characterizations may have reflected public posturing rather than the operational negotiating range. However, Steve Witkoff's public demand remains maximalist: Iran's enrichment facilities at Natanz, Fordow, and Isfahan must be dismantled — not merely suspended or placed under moratorium. This dismantlement demand is categorically different from a moratorium and remains the structural obstacle not addressed by the 12-15-year convergence. An opinion piece in multiple outlets flags that Trump has reportedly softened on whether Iran can retain any enriched uranium — a flip-flop with significant implications for the congressional zero-enrichment constraint. The Iran-US negotiations Wikipedia page and Slate's deal tracker confirm the MOU 30-day framework structure is still operative: deal would declare war's end, open a 30-day negotiation window on Hormuz transit, nuclear limits, and sanctions relief. Brent crude is at $106.92 and WTI at $100.59 — slightly off from Hormuz Day 82 highs but sustained above $100 on continued strait closure. Approximately 1,600 ships and 23,000 sailors remain stranded. Cumulative war cost last confirmed at $29 billion. WPA is at Day 23 past the April 29 statutory deadline; the 90-day hard deadline arrives May 29 — seven days out. At Day 90, any resumption of hostilities becomes definitionally unauthorized under any legal theory, including the administration's 'hostilities terminated' posture. Brent at $106.92 and WTI at $100.59 sustain the energy inflation component of the CPI/PPI trajectory. June FOMC is now 26 days out; the CME FedWatch tool shows approximately 98% hold probability. Warsh's first public communication — whenever it arrives — will set the market's anchor for the entire current inflation and war-cost cycle. Day 8 is not stabilization. items.headline: House GOP Cancels Iran War Powers Vote — Democrats Had Votes; Golden Flipping Yes; Next Attempt June — After 90-Day WPA Deadline; WPA Day 23
items.summary: The single most consequential domestic political development of May 22 is the House GOP's decision to cancel a scheduled Iran war powers resolution vote on May 21. The cancellation was caused by a demonstration vote on the Smithsonian American Women's History Museum construction bill that revealed eight Republican absences and six Republicans voting with Democrats — a procedural signal that the war powers resolution would pass. Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) — who has been the one consistent Democratic holdout against Iran war powers resolutions throughout the conflict — confirmed he was prepared to flip to yes, removing the last structural obstacle to a majority coalition. Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-NY), the resolution's sponsor, told reporters: 'No question about it, we would have succeeded.' House GOP leadership pulled the vote rather than absorb a defeat that would have constituted a bipartisan rebuke of presidential war-making. The next House attempt is now expected in early June, after the Memorial Day recess (which runs through May 26). This timing has a critical legal implication: the WPA 90-day hard deadline arrives May 29 — seven days from now. The next House vote comes after that deadline. The Senate remains without a scheduled 8th war powers resolution. The administration's 'hostilities terminated' legal posture — asserting that the pause stopped the 60-day WPA clock — does not survive scrutiny at Day 90 even on its own terms: the plain-text 90-day provision requires cessation of hostilities or congressional authorization, and the Hormuz closure with active naval blockade does not qualify as cessation. No resumption order was issued on May 22. The war continues on executive discretion past the April 29 statutory deadline and approaching the May 29 hard deadline. The bipartisan majority coalition now visible in the House — Rep. Golden flipping plus six Republicans plus Democrats — is the most significant constraint on executive war authority to materialize in the current conflict cycle. That it was pulled rather than voted on does not diminish its significance; it demonstrates that the coalition exists and can be mobilized. Its next mobilization attempt arrives after the 90-day deadline has passed, which changes the legal and political landscape fundamentally.
